<document>
# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
# Review: "Two Years On" (Varden and Halden follow-up)

This is a strong follow-up. It does the things the earlier documents most needed:
- it registered the mediation test before the outcomes were known;
- it added a second hours measure that doesn't depend on staff claiming time;
- it reports the counter-arm failure plainly, including its cost;
- it labels the Halden subset as "survivors twice over";
- it confirms what I suspected in reviewing the meta-analysis: all four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours.

The rebuttals of "entirely artifact" and "no sign of decay" are broadly fair.

Four issues need attention before the headline numbers can be relied on:
1. The decay estimate is confounded by changes in the control arm.
2. The Summary mixes a change of hours measure with a change over time.
3. It is unclear what the log measure actually counts, and this bears directly on the meetings result.
4. The mediation CIs probably overstate precision.

## Arithmetic check

| Figure | Check | |
|---|---|---|
| 0.966 / 0.88 | +9.8% (timesheets) | ✓ |
| 0.966 / 0.89 | +8.5% (logs) | ✓ |
| Halden: 34.9 / 40.3 | −13.4% | ✓ |
| Halden: 96.8 / 0.866 | +11.8% | ✓ |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 = 100 | ✓ |
| Meeting-time DiD | (3.9 − 7.4) − (7.0 − 7.2) = −3.3 h, matching month 6 | ✓ |
| "Declined by about a quarter" | 12.5 → 9.8 is −22%; 12.5 → 8.5 is −32% | Specify which comparison |
| Control meeting average, 7.2 → 7.0 | See §1 | Needs checking |

## 1. Control-arm changes confound the decay estimate

In month 15, two of the seven **control** offices cut standing meetings, and their output per hour then rose 4.1%. The paper presents this as a side observation. It is also contamination of the comparison group: control offices adopted part of the treatment.

- **Effect on the decay estimate.** When control offices improve, the DiD shrinks even if treated offices haven't changed. If the offices are roughly equal in size, two offices gaining 4.1% raises the control average by about 1.2 points. That is close to half of the 2.7-point decline from 12.5% to 9.8%, if the window covers those months.
- **"Consistent with some fading" may be partly wrong.** Some of the apparent fading may be the control arm catching up.
- **Likely information spillover.** The audits came after the nine-month report described meeting cuts. The authors should say whether the control offices knew of those findings.
- **A figure that may not fit.** If two control offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours of meetings, the control average should have fallen by about 0.6 hours, not 0.2. That is possible only if the other five control offices rose. Please confirm.

Requested analyses:
- treated and control trajectories reported separately;
- the 24-month DiD excluding the two audit offices, or censored at month 15;
- whether the 24-month estimate covers months 13–24 or is cumulative.

## 2. The Summary mixes a change of measure with a change over time

The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data." The 12.5% is a timesheet estimate; the 8.5% is a log estimate.

The like-for-like comparison is **12.5% → 9.8%**, as the body correctly says. The extra 1.3 points come from switching measures, not from the passage of time. The Summary overstates the decline.

Logs are also shown with no nine-month value, yet a DiD on log hours requires pre-period log data. Say whether logs were reconstructed back to baseline, and if so, report the nine-month log estimate as well.

## 3. What do the logs measure? This bears on the meetings result

The logs record "time staff are working on cases." Read literally, that excludes meetings. If so, the reported figures are hard to reconcile:

- Baseline was about 37.9 total hours, of which 7.4 were meetings, leaving about 30.5 hours outside meetings.
- At 24 months, total hours were about 33.4 and meetings 3.9, leaving about 29.5 hours outside meetings.
- Case-work time should therefore have fallen by **about 3%, not 11%**.

There are two possible readings, with different implications for the mediation result:

| If logs... | Then the meetings pathway is... |
|---|---|
| **include** meeting time (for example, staff stay logged in during meetings) | partly an **accounting identity**. Removing zero-output hours from the denominator mechanically raises output per hour. The cut is still a genuine gain, but "mediates 47%" mostly restates the arithmetic. |
| **exclude** meeting time | a **behavioural** channel, such as fewer interruptions or less fragmented work. That is a more interesting finding, but then the 11% fall needs explaining. |

The paper should state exactly what "active log-in time" counts. It should also report how much of the meetings share is arithmetic: what share would arise from removing 3.3 zero-output hours from the denominator, with no change in how productively the remaining hours are used? Using the earlier estimates, that arithmetic alone could plausibly account for most of the 47%.

## 4. Mediation: precision and independence

- **The sample is effectively seven treated offices.** "A larger sample of office-months" does not increase the effective sample, because months within an office are correlated. A CI of 28–66% for a mediated share estimated from 7 offices against 7 is very likely too narrow, unless the analysis accounts for clustering with a small-sample correction or randomisation inference. Report the method.
- **It tests the same offices again.** The registered test uses the same seven offices that generated the exploratory hypothesis, with overlapping months. Registration protects against flexible analysis. It does not answer Varga & Holm's replication concern, because there is no new sample.
- **The mediators are related.** Cutting meetings may itself reduce fatigue. If so, the separate shares depend on an assumption about which comes first.
- **Wording.** "Confirms" is too strong. "Is consistent with, in a pre-specified analysis" is more accurate. The limitation about unmeasured confounding of the mediators is stated, but the Summary should carry it too.

## 5. Small-cluster inference, still unaddressed

As I noted in my review of the nine-month report, 7-against-7 clustered CIs need a small-sample correction (wild cluster bootstrap or randomisation inference). The 8.5% CI of +3.4% to +13.8% will widen. It may still exclude zero, but "a clear margin" is premature until that is checked.

## 6. Cost, still missing

Case-processing offices still run about 3 hours a week above schedule, presumably as paid overtime, while output per FTE is −3.4%. Cost per case has therefore probably risen. The counter arm was ended *because of* a cost estimate (+9% per contact), yet the equivalent figure for the arm that continued is not reported. This is the number the county most needs.

The 9% figure also needs its basis. Twelve percent more staff giving 9% higher cost per contact implies labour is about 75% of cost, or some other assumption. Please state it.

## 7. Halden subset

- **The reversions include a discretionary organisation.** The Summary says all three reversions had "client-facing or coverage obligations." The marketing agency cited *client deadlines*, which is deadline-driven work, and the meta-analysis would classify it as discretionary. That is a meaningful exception to the work-type story and should be reported as one.
- **Non-response.** Nine of the 23 organisations contacted did not respond. Report what is known about them from the pilot data.
- **Secular trends.** The comparison spans about 2.5 years without a control group, during a period of fast adoption of AI and automation tools in professional services. That alone could produce several points of productivity growth. So the 11.8% may be biased upward even for self-selected survivors, and calling it an "upper bound" is not quite right.
- **Unaddressed attrition question.** R. Okafor is a Halden author and a co-author here. Varga & Holm reported that most of the "preparation-phase" withdrawals happened after the schedule began, and for workload reasons. This report should address that, since it bears on how Halden figures are used.

## 8. Smaller points

- **Sick days (−27%)** are still not adjusted for schedule structure. A four-day schedule mechanically lowers sick days per FTE by about 20%.
- **Appeals and resignations** are still raw rates, with no DiD or CIs. The appeal data are now less censored, which is good.
- **Characterisation of Varga & Holm.** They argued that energy would return to baseline "around month ten" (my calculation gives about 8.7) and that the residual gain was plausibly novelty. They did not forecast output per hour reaching zero at month ten. The rebuttal is fair in substance, but it should describe their argument accurately.
- **Endogenous continuation.** The counter arm ended at month 12, so only the arm that worked has 24-month data. That is a legitimate decision, but it means the "two-year" evidence applies to discretionary work only. The Summary should say so.
- **Reorganisation-only arm.** The paper rightly says the trial cannot separate reorganisation from hours. A three-arm follow-on (reduced hours; meeting reform at full hours; control) is the obvious next design and is worth recommending explicitly.

## Overall

The main conclusions survive:
- a per-hour gain of roughly 8–10% persists at two years in randomised, record-based, log-measured discretionary work;
- "entirely artifact" is refuted for this setting;
- the meta-analysis's no-decay claim rested on unsuitable studies.

Priorities:
1. Address control-arm contamination before interpreting the decline.
2. Correct the Summary's comparison across measures.
3. Define what the logs measure and separate the arithmetic part of the meetings mediation.
4. Use small-cluster inference throughout.
5. Report cost per case.

## Where the five documents now leave things

- **Discretionary work:** per-hour gains of roughly 8–10%, shrinking modestly over two years (by how much is uncertain because of contamination). Output per worker is about 3% below control, and cost per case is probably higher because of overtime.
- **Mechanism:** meeting reduction is the leading candidate. It may partly be removal of low-value hours rather than people working faster, and some of the gain may be available without cutting hours.
- **Coverage-bound work:** clear losses in output and service, with restoration costing about 9% per contact. Varden ended this arm.
- **Still open:** settings outside the public sector with controlled designs, effects beyond 24 months, and whether reorganisation alone can capture the gain.

I can draft a revised Summary for this report, or a one-page synthesis covering all five documents.
